clinicalPearls: A non-progressive, bilaterally symmetrical enlargement of the cornea with a normal intraocular pressure
The corneal diameter is enlarged beyond the normal range while the cornea remains clear
It is most often X-linked recessive, so it predominantly affects males
The crucial differential is primary congenital glaucoma (buphthalmos), which is distinguished by raised pressure, corneal oedema and progression
Associated features can include high myopia, lens subluxation, cataract and pigment dispersion
Management is largely refractive and monitoring, with attention to lens-related complications later in life
reference.pathophysiology: Megalocornea is a developmental enlargement of the cornea, thought to result from either an oversized optic cup or failure of the developing anterior segment to close normally, producing a large but structurally clear cornea with a deep anterior chamber. In the common X-linked form it is caused by mutations affecting anterior segment development. Unlike buphthalmos, the enlargement is not driven by raised intraocular pressure, so the cornea stays clear; however, the enlarged anterior segment can be associated with zonular weakness leading to lens subluxation and cataract.
additionalDifferentials: Marfan and other connective tissue disorders (for lens subluxation)
Anterior megalophthalmos as part of a syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of corneal diameter and intraocular pressure
Assessment for corneal clarity and Descemet tears (to exclude glaucoma)
Family history and, where appropriate, genetic evaluation
redFlags: Raised intraocular pressure or corneal oedema indicating glaucoma
Features of an underlying connective tissue disorder
reference.prognosis: Megalocornea itself is benign and non-progressive with generally good vision when refractive error is corrected; later lens complications may need intervention.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for primary congenital glaucoma and vice versa
Overlooking later lens subluxation or cataract
Attributing reduced vision solely to refractive error
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Correct the associated myopia and astigmatism with spectacles or contact lenses as the mainstay of care
Measure intraocular pressure and monitor serially to distinguish the benign condition from primary congenital glaucoma
Survey the lens and zonules for later subluxation and cataract
Undertake cataract and lens surgery when visually significant complications develop, anticipating zonular weakness
Reassure that the corneal enlargement is non-progressive with a generally good visual prognosis
Offer genetic counselling for the X-linked inheritance pattern that predominantly affects males
